Do not describe the whole CoA-containing molecule as having only two carbons; two-carbon refers to its acetyl cargo.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Objective W09-17 — CAC and complete accounting {#w09-lo17}

**Original objective:** What products are produced in one turn of the CAC and how many are produced (NADH, CO2, GTP) and what is the overall stoichiometry from glycolysis to CAC

Give one-turn CAC yield and then a stage-by-stage accounting of glycolysis, PDH and TWO CAC turns per glucose. Include FADH2 and distinguish ATP from GTP.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**One CAC turn:** 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2. **Glycolysis per glucose:** 2 NADH, net 2 ATP, no CO2. **PDH per glucose:** 2 NADH and 2 CO2. **Two CAC turns:** 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 GTP and 4 CO2. **Overall:** 10 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP + 2 GTP (4 ATP equivalents) and 6 CO2. No oxidative-phosphorylation ATP conversion factor is needed here.

**Source:** Week 9 objectives, item 17; Lecture 9:25–9:26; Tutorial 6, PDF pp. 4–5.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-lo17 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Build the total from separate stage rows and keep the counting basis explicit. Two CAC turns contribute six NADH, two FADH2, two GTP and four CO2; then add glycolysis and PDH. The four ATP equivalents here are two ATP plus two GTP, not ATP calculated from oxidative phosphorylation.

Build the answer in layers. One CAC turn gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, and 2 CO2. Because one glucose supplies two acetyl-CoA entries, two turns give **6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 GTP, and 4 CO2**. Add the earlier stages without changing their boundaries: glycolysis contributes 2 NADH and net 2 ATP; PDH contributes 2 NADH and 2 CO2.

The carrier sum is **2 + 2 + 6 = 10 NADH**, with **2 FADH2** kept separate. The CO2 sum is **0 + 2 + 4 = 6**. The directly formed nucleotide total is **2 ATP + 2 GTP**, commonly expressed here as four ATP equivalents.

That last phrase does not include ATP later obtained by oxidative phosphorylation. No ATP-per-NADH factor belongs in this question. The carbon result is net pathway accounting and should not be used to claim the precise timing of release of individually labeled acetyl carbons.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Objective W09-18 — Anaplerotic reactions {#w09-lo18}

**Original objective:** What is an anapleurotic reaction with respect to the CAC

Define anaplerotic reaction and explain why a cycle needs replenishment when intermediates are withdrawn.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An anaplerotic reaction refills a CAC intermediate removed for biosynthesis, maintaining the pool needed for continued cycling. The lecture emphasizes that amino-acid carbon skeletons can feed into several CAC intermediates. “Anapleurotic” is the original sheet's spelling; “anaplerotic” is the term used here.

**Source:** Week 9 objectives, item 18; Lecture 9, anaplerotic-reaction discussion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-lo18 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A closed-looking cycle diagram can hide withdrawals to biosynthesis. Once material leaves, continued cycling requires replenishment of its intermediate pool. That is the purpose of anaplerosis; the lecture's amino-acid carbon skeletons illustrate possible inputs.

The apparent puzzle is why a cycle that regenerates its acceptor needs anything replenished. The answer is that the biological system is not a perfectly closed loop: intermediates can be diverted into biosynthetic pathways. Once material leaves, internal regeneration alone does not replace that withdrawal. Anaplerotic reactions restore input to the intermediate pool.

The lecture illustrates this with amino-acid carbon skeletons entering at different CAC positions. Their significance here is replenishment, not a claim that every amino acid enters at the same point or that NADH is directly turned into ATP. Also distinguish acetyl-CoA entry from replacement of withdrawn intermediates; they are not interchangeable descriptions. The objective sheet's spelling is retained in the original question, while the model answer uses anaplerotic for the concept being explained.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Objective W09-19 — Lactate and NAD+ regeneration {#w09-lo19}

**Original objective:** Under what conditions is pyruvate converted to lactate and why?

Explain the condition, redox partners, regenerated carrier and effect on glycolysis and ATP yield.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In oxygen-limited muscle, respiratory reoxidation of NADH is inadequate. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to **NAD+**. Regenerated NAD+ allows the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step to continue. Lactate formation does not itself add ATP; continuing glycolysis supplies net two ATP per glucose.

**Source:** Week 9 objectives, item 19; Lecture 9, anaerobic glycolysis; Tutorial 6.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-lo19 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The redox bottleneck explains the lactate response. When respiratory NADH reoxidation is inadequate, pyruvate accepts its electrons and NAD+ is restored for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate oxidation. Lactate formation enables continued glycolytic ATP production but does not itself increase the ATP yield per glucose.

Start at the requirement that becomes difficult to maintain. The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate oxidation step needs NAD+ to accept reducing equivalents. In the oxygen-limited muscle situation described, respiratory reoxidation does not restore NAD+ rapidly enough. Lactate dehydrogenase provides the alternative transfer: pyruvate accepts reducing equivalents and becomes lactate, while NADH is oxidized to NAD+.

The regenerated NAD+ allows the glycolytic oxidation step to continue, supporting the later substrate-level ATP-producing reactions. The lactate reaction itself is not an extra ATP-producing step, so the overall glycolytic gain remains net two ATP per glucose. Do not say that glycolysis directly consumes oxygen or that lactate is made mainly to release CO2. The causal chain is inadequate carrier reoxidation, alternative NAD+ regeneration, continued glycolysis, and preservation of its limited ATP yield.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Objective W09-20 — Cori cycle {#w09-lo20}

**Original objective:** What is the Cori Cycle?

Describe the complete muscle–blood–liver–blood route and name the liver process.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Muscle produces lactate during anaerobic glycolysis. Lactate enters blood and is taken up by the liver, where gluconeogenesis converts its carbon back into glucose. Glucose returns through the circulation and can fuel muscle again. This is a two-organ exchange, not conversion of lactate to extra ATP in the muscle.

**Source:** Week 9 objectives, item 20; Lecture 9, Cori cycle; Tutorial 6, PDF p. 8.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-lo20 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Trace carbon between tissues, not merely between two metabolites in one cell. Lactate travels from muscle to liver, the liver performs gluconeogenesis and glucose returns in blood. Including both transport legs explains why this is an inter-organ cycle.

Follow carbon through the full inter-organ route. Muscle converts glucose through glycolysis to pyruvate and then to lactate in the anaerobic example. Lactate leaves muscle, enters the blood, and reaches the liver. In the liver, **gluconeogenesis** converts that carbon back toward glucose. Glucose is released into the circulation and can return to muscle as fuel.

Both transport legs are part of the answer: muscle-to-liver as lactate and liver-to-muscle as glucose. Omitting one leaves an incomplete cycle. The liver process is glucose synthesis, not simply reversing the lactate reaction inside muscle to obtain extra ATP. This question tests coordination between tissues as well as the names of the metabolites, so label the organs, transported molecules, and liver process explicitly.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

# Part C — Integrated Practice

### Integrated Question 1 — Carbon accounting
Why does everything after glycolysis reaction 4 need to be counted twice per glucose?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Because the six-carbon glucose has been split into two three-carbon molecules. Both molecules pass through the remaining payoff reactions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-ix01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The factor of two begins with splitting a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon units. Following the rearrangement, both continue through the payoff sequence. Counting only one would halve the downstream products per glucose.

Before cleavage, a reaction acts on one six-carbon molecule per original glucose. Cleavage creates two three-carbon pieces, and reaction 5 brings the relevant pair into the form that continues as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Each of those two molecules then goes through the payoff sequence. A yield stated per three-carbon substrate must therefore be multiplied by two to express it per glucose.

For example, one NADH formed from each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate gives two NADH per glucose. Similarly, an ATP-producing payoff reaction acting once on each of the two intermediates gives two ATP per glucose. This factor does not retroactively double reactions 1 and 3, which took place before the split. The original wording groups the cleavage-and-rearrangement stage; the useful precision is that both three-carbon units proceed through the payoff reactions after that stage. State both the structural reason and the accounting consequence, rather than treating the factor of two as an arbitrary rule.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 2 — Redox and ATP
Why is reaction 6 important even though it does not directly make ATP?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It captures electrons in NADH and creates 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, whose high transfer potential drives ATP formation in reaction 7.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-ix02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A step can prepare an energy-capturing reaction without directly making ATP. Reaction 6 captures electrons in NADH and forms 1,3-BPG, which supplies the phosphate for reaction 7. Keeping preparation and direct ATP formation separate explains the significance of both steps.

There are two kinds of energy capture to identify. First, oxidation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate transfers reducing equivalents to NAD+, making NADH. Second, formation of 1,3-BPG creates an intermediate with sufficiently high phosphate-transfer potential to support the next ATP-producing reaction. Reaction 6 therefore prepares a chemical route for direct ATP formation even though ATP is not its immediate product in the step-by-step account.

Reaction 7 completes that part of the sequence by transferring phosphate from 1,3-BPG to ADP. Saying reaction 6 directly makes ATP merges two different steps; saying it is unimportant because it makes no ATP ignores both NADH capture and the preparation of 1,3-BPG. Continued turnover also requires replacement of NADH by fresh NAD+ and regeneration of the oxidized-carrier pool. The explanation should preserve the existing source note about the lecture's label while keeping the two numbered reactions distinct.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 3 — Anaerobic logic
If lactate dehydrogenase were blocked during intense oxygen-limited exercise, which glycolytic requirement would become limiting?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**NAD+** would become limiting. Without lactate formation, NADH could not be efficiently reoxidized to regenerate NAD+, causing glycolysis to stall at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-ix03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Under the stated oxygen limitation, blocking lactate dehydrogenase removes the route used to recycle NADH to NAD+. The glycolytic oxidation step then lacks its electron acceptor. The predicted bottleneck is NAD+ availability, not a direct requirement that glycolysis consume oxygen.

Use the condition in the question rather than assuming respiratory recycling can make up the difference. During the stated intense, oxygen-limited exercise, NADH cannot be reoxidized adequately through the respiratory route. Lactate dehydrogenase normally transfers reducing equivalents from NADH to pyruvate, regenerating NAD+ as lactate forms. Blocking that reaction removes the compensating route described in the course.

As available NAD+ becomes limiting, the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step loses the oxidized electron acceptor it requires. Slowing that step reduces continuation through the payoff sequence and threatens glycolytic ATP supply. The immediate bottleneck asked for is therefore **NAD+**, not a shortage of oxygen as a direct glycolytic substrate and not a requirement that lactate itself donate phosphate to ADP. The conclusion is conditional on the oxygen-limited situation specified; the question is not asking for an unrestricted claim about all tissues under every condition.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 4 — Pathway synthesis
Trace one glucose molecule from glucose through the end of the CAC in one sentence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Glucose is split by glycolysis into two pyruvates, each pyruvate is converted by PDH to acetyl-CoA, and the two acetyl-CoA molecules drive two CAC turns that release the remaining carbons as CO2 while producing NADH, FADH2, and GTP.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w09-ix04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Use the carbon-entry sequence as the backbone of the sentence: one glucose, two pyruvates, two acetyl-CoA entries and two CAC turns. Attach carrier and CO2 production to that sequence. The statement describes overall pathway accounting, not a requirement to follow individual labeled carbon atoms through one cycle turn.

Use a single carbon-flow backbone and attach the products to the appropriate stages. One glucose undergoes glycolysis to produce two pyruvates. PDH converts each pyruvate into one acetyl-CoA, giving two acetyl entries into the CAC. Two turns supply the per-glucose cycle output. This sequence explains why the multiplicity changes from one starting glucose to two downstream entries.

The summary should not imply that pyruvate enters the CAC unchanged or that PDH belongs inside glycolysis. It should also preserve the difference between the carrier products NADH and FADH2 and the directly formed GTP. The CO2 statement is a net accounting statement for the connected pathway, not a tracing experiment showing that every original carbon is released on its first passage through the cycle. A one-sentence response can be compact, but understanding these boundaries is what makes that sentence accurate rather than merely a memorized list of pathway names.

**Review:** [Week 9 study guide](../study-guides/week09-glycolysis-cac.qmd).
:::
